headline: Light showers hang on through Sunday, then a much stormier stretch starts Tuesday with repeated rounds of rain, mountain snow and gusty winds, plus a growing coastal flooding threat.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: A slow-moving low-pressure system parked offshore keeps spinning periods of light rain showers into the north Olympic Peninsula, the Strait shoreline and the Puget Sound lowlands this Saturday evening and tonight, with light snow in the mountains. Clouds thicken and lower overnight, lowest in the south interior. Lows fall into the 30s to low 40s; forecasters say the forecast is on track.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Light showers linger into Sunday while a blocking pattern keeps the weather stuck in place, and clouds lift by Sunday afternoon. Sunday night into Monday the rain turns steadier, starting over the Olympics and spreading inland, with snow levels starting around 2,000–3,000 feet and rising Monday; a Winter Weather Advisory runs from 6 PM Sunday to 4 PM Monday for the Olympics, including Hurricane Ridge, where 5–10 inches of snow is forecast. A brief break is possible Monday evening before the next front arrives late Monday night into Tuesday. Highs stay near normal in the upper 40s to low 50s, with lows in the 30s to low 40s.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: The offshore low deepens Tuesday and sends a series of storm systems across western Washington, bringing multiple rounds of widespread lowland rain, mountain snow and gusty winds from Tuesday through the second half of the week. Rivers will start to rise; widespread river flooding is not expected, but the Skokomish River will likely reach minor flood stage around midweek onward.

coast: A Coastal Flood Advisory runs from 7 AM to 3 PM Sunday for the Grays Harbor County and northern Washington coasts, as larger high tides plus storm surge and wave action bring flooding concerns back with Sunday's high tide (conditions on the north coast are more marginal). Water levels climb further Monday onward, and Tuesday's storm brings another round of high surf. Confidence is growing that moderate to major coastal flooding could occur along parts of the Grays Harbor County coast during the Tuesday and Wednesday high tides. Tides also rise significantly along the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Puget Sound shorelines from Tuesday onward, and impacts there will be closely monitored. On the water, a Small Craft Advisory runs until 10 AM Sunday for the east entrance of the Strait and until 4 AM Monday for the coastal waters, with seas building to about 12–14 feet by early Sunday. A Gale Watch covers the coastal waters from late Sunday night through Tuesday afternoon: advisory-strength winds return late Sunday, with a 40–60% chance of gales Monday night into Tuesday and a 30% chance of storm-force gusts over the outer coastal waters; another storm late Wednesday brings perhaps the best chance of storm-force winds offshore. Seas above 16 feet are likely Tuesday and Wednesday, with about a 40% chance of 20-foot seas and confused, mixed swell.
watch_for: Possible moderate to major coastal flooding on the Grays Harbor County coast with the Tuesday and Wednesday high tides, and rising tides along the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Puget Sound from Tuesday on.
The stormy stretch from Tuesday through late week: widespread rain, mountain snow and gusty winds.
The Skokomish River, likely reaching minor flood stage around midweek.
confidence: Forecasters are confident in light showers through Sunday, the Olympics snow Sunday night into Monday and a turn to a stormier pattern from Tuesday, while coastal flooding along the Strait and Puget Sound later in the week remains less certain.
